extracted.intended_audience: general readers, travelers, and agricultural reformers / American farmers
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a 19th-century travel narrative containing prescriptive agricultural and rural-improvement advice observed in Lombardy (irrigation, tree-planting, water-power use, vine training, and cooperative works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrigation
rubrics_metrics.description: American Agriculture has just two arts to learn from Lombardy—Irrigation and Tree-Planting. Nearly all our great intervales might be irrigated immensely to the profit of their cultivators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrigation returns fertility otherwise lost to running water and can increase productiveness year to year; the valley of the Nile is cited as an example of what irrigation from rivers at their highest stage will do for soil. Even where a head of water is not naturally available, water might be profitably lifted and distributed through canals or ditches. Where a head of water can supply power, the cost after first outlay need not be considerable; even steam-power and contemporary pumping machinery could make irrigation profitable in many places. Specific local examples include using turbid streams and marshy ponds (e.g., parts of New-Jersey and Long Island) to double yields. The author also notes that much fertilizing matter is currently squandered to the ocean (Raritan, Passaic etc.) and could be conserved by irrigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tree-Planting
rubrics_metrics.description: As to Tree-Planting, there can be no excuse for neglecting it... There is scarcely a farm of fifty acres or over in any but the very newest States that might not be increased in value $1,000 by $100 judiciously expended in Tree-Planting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant road-sides, steep hill-sides, ravines and rocky places with Oak, Hickory, Chestnut, Pine, Locust, etc.; protect young trees from premature destruction. Utility, beauty, comfort and profit all argue for immediate and extensive tree-planting. By planting fast-growing species (e.g., Locust) alternately with slower growers (Oak, Hickory), the former can be ready for use or sale by the time the latter need the ground. A well-managed planting might yield $100 worth of timber annually without materially reducing crop area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective/cooperative irrigation (Association)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten thousand farms together, embracing a whole valley, may often be irrigated for less than the cost of supplying a hundred of them separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pooling resources and organizing irrigation collectively dramatically reduces per-farm cost. The author suggests organizing large-scale works (dams, canals) potentially employing immigrant labor (e.g., proposing 100,000 immigrants for New Jersey projects) to accomplish valley-wide irrigation more cheaply than piecemeal efforts. Agricultural press and local agitation are recommended to promote such cooperative improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use canals and irrigation water for mechanical and manufacturing power
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of Lombardy slopes very considerably toward the Po, so that the water in the larger or distributing canals is often used to run mills and supply other mechanical power. It might be used also for Manufacturing if Manufactures existed here, and nearly every farmer might have a horse-power or so at command for domestic uses if he chose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canal water can drive grist-mills and other machinery even where natural streams are dry; examples cited of mills grinding where no river naturally existed. Encourages thinking beyond mere irrigation to harnessing water for local manufacturing and domestic mechanical power, expanding rural productive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vine training and local orchard practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vine is very generally trained on a low tree, like one of our Plum or small Cherry trees, so that, viewed at a distance or a point near the ground, the country would seem one vast forest, with an undergrowth mainly of Wheat and Indian Corn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vine-training methods observed include training vines on low trees, on stakes, and rarely on dwarf trees. Mulberry, Poplar, Walnut, Cherry and similar trees are commonly grown along canals, brooks, roads and across fields, forming an integrated landscape. These practices influence both aesthetics and productive layout of farms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of poor cultivation practices (crowding and bad hoeing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indian Corn will be where it is not prevented by the vicious crowding of the plants and sugar-loaf hoeing of which I have frequently spoken. With Potatoes, nearly the same mistake is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author attributes much lower yields to poor cultivation techniques—overcrowding of plants and inappropriate hoeing methods—which result in substantially reduced productivity. Implicit guidance: adopt better spacing and cultivation methods to increase yields, as Italy realizes less than half the yield she would with judicious cultivation.
